statement: A photograph is enlarged so that each side becomes 3 times as long. How many times bigger is its area?

choices.misconception: I applied the length scale factor straight to the area.
I doubled the scale factor because area involves two dimensions, instead of squaring it.
I multiplied the scale factor by four, as though area scaled with the number of sides.
I cubed the scale factor, which is the rule for volume rather than area.

hints: Try it on a small rectangle first.
Take a rectangle you can compute, triple both sides, and compare the two areas. The relationship you find holds for any shape, not just that rectangle.
A 2 by 5 rectangle has area 10. Tripled it becomes 6 by 15 with area 90, which is 9 times as much. Area scales by the square of the length factor.

solutions.reliable: Test it concretely. A 2 by 5 rectangle has area 10. After tripling each side it is 6 by 15, with area 90 - nine times the original. In general, tripling both dimensions multiplies the area by 3 x 3 = 9. The transferable idea: length scales by k, area by k squared, volume by k cubed.
solutions.elegant: Nine copies of the original photo tile the enlarged one exactly, three across and three down.

whyOnTest: Applying a length scale factor to an area is one of the highest-frequency errors across the whole exam, at every band.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
